domain_label: External-Integration & Platform-Ops: Reliability & Base44 Platform Operations
purpose: The runtime discipline for making every effect that crosses the app boundary durable, safe-to-retry, and observable — distributed-systems reliability (idempotency keys, backoff retries, durable outbox/queue, dead-letter, circuit breaker, timeout budgets) extended across the network boundary from sysloops' append-only/idempotent rules, executed on the Base44 platform (Deno backend functions, scheduled Automations, per-app Secrets for user API keys, agents-as-JSONC, 2-way GitHub sync) as the runtime half of the managing agent.
assumptions: no observed dataset or live Base44 project supplied; all scores are heuristic priors and Base44/vendor behaviors are taken from EXTERNAL_RECON snippet-verified facts, not from running the platform

the app is the single-user study system whose sysloops specialist already owns the loop DOCTRINE (idempotency, append-only, degraded mode, metric governance); this KB owns only the RUNTIME implementation of those rules across the network boundary on Base44

external service specifics (AnkiConnect, Ollama Cloud, Google Calendar/Tasks, WAHA) are cited from EXTERNAL_RECON; where a needed platform limit (Base44 function execution/rate limits, Ollama rate limits) is not in recon it is carried as a named UNKNOWN with a METHOD, never invented

the specialist's other two KBs own the per-integration API surface details and LLM model-ops depth; this KB stays on reliability primitives plus Base44 platform ops and only names integrations as reliability examples
exclusions: the full per-endpoint API surface of each integration (AnkiConnect action catalog, Ollama endpoint list, Google event fields, WAHA session lifecycle) beyond naming them as reliability examples — owned by the integration KB
LLM model selection/evaluation/drift science in depth (prompt quality, eval rubrics) beyond the runtime fallback/retirement/cost-tracking wiring — owned by the model-ops KB slice
the sysloops nightly-analysis pipeline's ANALYTICAL steps (calibration, re-fit, diagnosis, planning) beyond hosting that pipeline as an idempotent scheduled Base44 Automation
UI/UX of settings screens where a user pastes keys or grants OAuth consent — owned by the uxguide specialist
multi-user auth, tenant isolation, and app-security hardening (single-user app; premature per SPECIALIST_LIST gaps 9/11)

competency_questions.question: What failure modes appear when an effect crosses the app boundary to an external service, and why is exactly-once delivery unachievable?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: names timeouts, partial failure, duplicate delivery and the ambiguous-outcome problem, states that exactly-once is unachievable so the system targets at-least-once delivery made safe by idempotency, and ties this to extending sysloops' append-only rule across the network

competency_questions.question: How does an idempotency key make a retried external mutation safe against double-application?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: defines a client-generated idempotency key attached to each mutation so a server dedupes replays within a window, and gives AnkiConnect allowDuplicate/duplicateScope as the domain example of server-side dedupe

competency_questions.question: What is a correct retry-with-backoff policy, which errors are retriable, and how do timeout budgets bound it?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: prescribes exponential backoff with jitter, a max-attempt cap, retrying only transient errors (timeouts, 5xx, 429 honoring Retry-After) and never non-idempotent 4xx, and bounds each attempt with a per-call timeout smaller than the enclosing function budget

competency_questions.question: Why persist intent in a durable outbox/queue before calling an external service?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: explains that appending the intended effect to a durable append-only store before the external call means a crash or restart cannot lose the effect, decouples the user action from external latency, and lets a worker drain and retry

competency_questions.question: How are repeated failures and poison messages handled without blocking the queue or hammering a downed dependency?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: routes messages exceeding max attempts to a dead-letter/flagged state for review so they do not block the queue, and trips a circuit breaker to fail fast and degrade gracefully when a dependency is persistently failing

competency_questions.question: What are Base44 backend functions and why must every external API call run inside one?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: states backend functions run custom TypeScript on Deno in an isolated environment for business logic, third-party calls with protected credentials, webhooks and custom endpoints, and that this is the only place a cloud app can safely hold secrets and reach external services

competency_questions.question: How do Base44 Automations turn the sysloops nightly pipeline into a real scheduled loop, and what must hold for overlapping runs?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: states Automations run backend functions on schedules or on DB create/update/delete events, that this is the runtime for the nightly pipeline, and that scheduled runs must be idempotent and guarded against overlap

competency_questions.question: How are user-provided API keys stored and used via per-app Secrets, and how are they rotated and protected?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: describes storing pasted keys as per-app Secrets (env vars) read only inside backend functions, never exposed to the client, and a rotation/revocation/least-privilege lifecycle that keeps secrets out of logs and out of the GitHub-synced repo

competency_questions.question: How are agents defined as JSONC and version-controlled through Base44's 2-way GitHub sync, and what is the sync risk?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: states agents are JSONC config under base44/agents/ synced via the Base44 CLI, that Base44 edits auto-commit and GitHub pushes reflect back (Builder plan+), and that the two-way sync must never carry secrets and needs conflict discipline

competency_questions.question: Why can a cloud app never reach AnkiConnect directly, and how is Anki sync made reliable across that gap?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: states AnkiConnect binds 127.0.0.1:8765 and needs Anki running so a cloud backend can only reach it via a bridge on the user's machine, and prescribes queuing writes while Anki is offline and reconciling with idempotent addNote when it returns

competency_questions.question: Why do Google Calendar/Tasks require OAuth rather than a pasted key, and how is timed-reminder delivery handled?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: states private-calendar access needs per-user OAuth 2.0 consent (not an API key), that tokens must be stored/refreshed and re-consented on revoke, and that timed reminders use Calendar event reminder overrides because the Tasks API discards the due time

competency_questions.question: How is LLM model-ops made resilient to model retirement, provider failure, and the two-active-model limit?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: prescribes pinning to non-retiring recommended models, a fallback chain behind retries and the circuit breaker, and cost/latency tracking, noting the 2026-07-15 Ollama retirements and the two-active-cloud-models constraint as facts to build around

competency_questions.question: How does every external call earn an observability metric with a named consumer?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: requires each external call to emit success-rate/latency/retry-count/DLQ-depth snapshots with a threshold and a named automatic action or human-visible flag, deleting any metric with no consumer, extending sysloops' metric governance across the boundary

competency_questions.question: What is the recommended reliability and Base44 ops stack, and what is explicitly out (go/no-go)?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: commits to idempotency keys + backoff retries + durable outbox + DLQ + circuit breaker + timeout budgets on Base44 backend functions and Automations with per-app Secrets, Anki via a localhost bridge queue, Google via OAuth, model-ops fallback, and no-gos: no direct cloud-to-AnkiConnect, no secrets in the synced repo, WAHA off by default, and idempotent-verified webhook handling

glossary.definition: A client-generated identifier attached to an external mutation so that a retried or duplicated request is applied at most once: the server (or a dedupe store) recognizes the key and returns the original result instead of re-executing. It is what turns unavoidable at-least-once delivery into a safe effective-exactly-once; AnkiConnect's allowDuplicate/duplicateScope options are a concrete server-side dedupe surface [FACT-source: EXTERNAL_RECON §2].

A retry schedule where the wait between attempts grows exponentially (e.g. base * 2^n) with added randomness (jitter) to avoid synchronized retry storms, capped at a max attempt count; applied only to transient errors (timeouts, 5xx, 429) and honoring a server's Retry-After [METHOD — standard reliability practice].

Persisting the INTENT of an external effect to a durable append-only store before attempting the call, so a crash or restart replays the intent rather than losing it; a worker drains the store, calls the service with an idempotency key, and marks the row done — the network-boundary extension of sysloops' append-only rule.

A holding location for messages that exceed their max retry budget (poison messages), moved out of the main queue so they neither block healthy traffic nor retry forever; DLQ contents are surfaced for human review or a repair job.

A guard that, after a threshold of failures to a dependency, 'opens' to fail fast (skip calls) for a cooldown before a half-open trial, preventing a downed or slow service from exhausting timeouts and cascading; the runtime form of sysloops' degraded mode.

Custom TypeScript run on Deno in an isolated Base44 environment for business logic, third-party API calls with protected credentials, webhooks and custom endpoints; the only place a Base44 cloud app can hold secrets and reach external services [FACT-source: EXTERNAL_RECON §6].

A Base44 backend function triggered on a schedule or on database create/update/delete events; the mechanism that turns the app's runPipeline into a real recurring scheduled loop [FACT-source: EXTERNAL_RECON §6].

A Base44-stored environment variable (e.g. a user-pasted Ollama/Tripo/WAHA/Google key) readable only inside backend functions and never exposed to the client; external services do not auto-share credentials, the user pastes them and Base44 injects them at call time [FACT-source: EXTERNAL_RECON §6].

Base44 AI agents defined declaratively as JSONC config files under base44/agents/ and synced via the Base44 CLI; the version-controllable, reviewable definition of the managing agent's runtime wiring [FACT-source: EXTERNAL_RECON §6].

A component running on the user's own machine that a cloud backend talks to because AnkiConnect binds 127.0.0.1:8765 and requires the desktop Anki app running; the cloud app can never reach AnkiConnect directly, only via this bridge [FACT-source: EXTERNAL_RECON §2 and §Cross-cutting].

nodes.definition: Frame the problem: the moment an effect leaves the app process for another service (Ollama, Anki, Google, WAHA, GitHub), it crosses a network boundary where the process can no longer guarantee the effect happened. Reliability engineering here means making every cross-boundary effect DURABLE (survives a crash), IDEMPOTENT (safe to repeat), and OBSERVABLE (its outcome is recorded) — the direct extension of sysloops' append-only/idempotent nightly-loop rules across the network [FACT — sysloops idempotent/append-only doctrine per SPECIALIST_LIST §A9/§B2; the cross-boundary framing is design synthesis, ESTIMATE]. Everything downstream (keys, backoff, outbox, breakers) is a mechanism serving these three properties; the platform that hosts them is Base44.

included: the durable/idempotent/observable objective for cross-boundary effects
the extension of sysloops' append-only rule across the network
the framing that hosts the reliability primitives
excluded: the specific failure taxonomy (its own node)
any per-service API detail

pros.claim: Stating durable+idempotent+observable as the three properties gives every later mechanism a single reason to exist and a test to meet
pros.example: justifying the outbox as the durability mechanism and idempotency keys as the repeat-safety mechanism rather than as unrelated features

cons.claim: The frame is a design synthesis over sysloops doctrine, not a measured contract, so the exact boundary of what counts as an effect is a judgment
cons.example: debating whether a read-only Ollama model-list call needs the same durability treatment as a write to Anki

failure_modes: treating an external call like an in-process call and assuming it either fully succeeded or fully failed
adding reliability mechanisms with no stated property they serve
acceptance_tests: the frame names durable, idempotent and observable as the three cross-boundary properties and ties them to sysloops' append-only/idempotent rule
revisit_triggers: sysloops changes its idempotency/append-only doctrine
a new class of external effect appears that the three-property frame does not cover
the app moves off Base44

base.update_signal: a change in sysloops doctrine or a move off Base44 revises the frame

nodes.definition: Enumerate what actually goes wrong across the boundary: connection timeouts, slow responses, partial failure (the call landed but the acknowledgment was lost — the AMBIGUOUS-OUTCOME problem), duplicate delivery, and dependency outage. From these follows the delivery-semantics truth: exactly-once delivery is unachievable over an unreliable network, so the system targets AT-LEAST-ONCE delivery and makes it safe with idempotency, rather than pretending at-most-once (which silently loses effects) [FACT — standard distributed-systems result; framing is METHOD]. The ambiguous timeout is the central case: a write that times out may or may not have applied, so blind retry can double-apply unless the mutation is idempotent.

included: the timeout/partial-failure/duplicate/outage taxonomy
the ambiguous-outcome problem
at-least-once-plus-idempotency as the chosen semantics
excluded: the idempotency-key mechanism (its own node)
the retry schedule (its own node)

pros.claim: Naming the ambiguous-outcome case explicitly forces every write path to answer 'is this safe to repeat?' before it ships
pros.example: recognizing that an addNote that timed out might already be in Anki, so the retry needs a dedupe key not a blind resend

cons.claim: The taxonomy is generic and does not by itself say which failures a given vendor actually emits, so per-service error mapping is still required
cons.example: not knowing whether a Base44 backend-function timeout to Ollama returns a distinguishable transient error or a generic 500

failure_modes: assuming a timeout means the write did not happen
choosing at-most-once semantics and silently dropping effects to avoid duplicates
acceptance_tests: the taxonomy lists timeout, partial failure, duplicate delivery and outage, names the ambiguous-outcome case, and states at-least-once-plus-idempotency as the semantics because exactly-once is unachievable
revisit_triggers: a vendor's observed error behavior contradicts the assumed taxonomy
a new integration adds a failure mode not listed
delivery-semantics requirements change for a specific effect

base.update_signal: an observed vendor error behavior or a new integration changes the taxonomy

nodes.definition: Make every external mutation safe to repeat by attaching a stable, client-generated idempotency key (e.g. a UUID derived from the logical action, not the attempt) so a retry carries the SAME key and the server or a dedupe store applies the effect at most once, returning the original result for replays within a dedupe window [FACT — standard idempotency-key pattern; METHOD for the derivation]. Where a service exposes native dedupe, use it: AnkiConnect's addNote takes options.allowDuplicate and options.duplicateScope so a re-sent note is not duplicated [FACT-source: EXTERNAL_RECON §2]; where it does not, keep an app-side ledger of applied keys. This is the mechanism that makes the at-least-once semantics safe.

included: the client-generated stable key attached to each mutation
server-side dedupe (AnkiConnect allowDuplicate/duplicateScope) vs an app-side applied-key ledger
the dedupe-window concept
excluded: the retry schedule that reuses the key (its own node)
the outbox that stores the key alongside intent (its own node)

pros.claim: A stable key reused across attempts converts an unsafe blind retry into a safe replay with no double-application
pros.example: resending a timed-out addNote with the same key so Anki dedupes it instead of creating two identical cards

cons.claim: Not every external service honors a client key or exposes native dedupe, forcing an app-side ledger that must itself be durable and bounded
cons.example: a service with no idempotency support where the app must remember every applied key long enough to cover the retry window

failure_modes: deriving the key per attempt instead of per logical action so retries look like new requests
assuming a service dedupes when it does not and double-applying
acceptance_tests: the key is defined as stable per logical action and reused across retries, native dedupe (AnkiConnect allowDuplicate/duplicateScope) is preferred with an app-side ledger fallback, and a replay is shown to return the original result not a second effect
revisit_triggers: a service changes or drops its dedupe support
the app-side key ledger grows unbounded
the dedupe window proves too short for the retry schedule

base.update_signal: a dropped vendor dedupe or an unbounded key ledger changes the idempotency mechanism

nodes.definition: Retry transient failures with EXPONENTIAL BACKOFF plus jitter (wait grows as base*2^n with randomness) up to a max-attempt cap, and retry ONLY errors that are safe and likely to succeed later: timeouts, 5xx, and 429 rate-limits honoring any Retry-After header — never a non-idempotent 4xx (a 400/401/403 will not fix itself and a blind retry of a non-idempotent write duplicates the effect) [FACT — standard retry practice; METHOD for the exact schedule]. Retries presuppose an idempotency key so a replay of an ambiguously-failed write is safe. Jitter prevents synchronized retry storms; the cap prevents unbounded amplification of a downed dependency's load.

included: exponential backoff with jitter and a max-attempt cap
the retriable (timeout/5xx/429) vs terminal (non-idempotent 4xx) classification
honoring Retry-After
excluded: the circuit breaker that stops retrying entirely (its own node)
the DLQ that catches exhausted retries (its own node)

pros.claim: Backoff with jitter and a cap absorbs transient blips without amplifying load on a struggling dependency
pros.example: a 429 from Ollama Cloud waited out with growing, jittered delays instead of an immediate hammering resend

cons.claim: Misclassifying a terminal error as retriable wastes quota and delays surfacing a real fault; retries without idempotency duplicate writes
cons.example: retrying a 401 from an expired Google token four times before the user ever sees the re-consent prompt

failure_modes: retrying a non-idempotent write with no key and duplicating the effect
retrying a permanent 4xx and masking a configuration fault
acceptance_tests: the policy specifies exponential backoff with jitter and a cap, retries only timeouts/5xx/429 honoring Retry-After, never a non-idempotent 4xx, and requires an idempotency key on any retried mutation
revisit_triggers: retry storms or rising 429s are observed
a vendor's error codes are re-mapped
the max-attempt cap proves too low or too high in practice

base.update_signal: an observed retry storm or a vendor error re-map changes the retry policy

nodes.definition: Persist the INTENT of every external effect to a durable append-only store (an outbox row: logical action, idempotency key, payload, status) BEFORE attempting the call, then let a worker drain the store, execute the call, and mark the row done — so a crash between user action and external call replays the intent rather than losing it, and slow external latency never blocks the user path [FACT — outbox/transactional-queue pattern; the append-only tie is sysloops doctrine per SPECIALIST_LIST §B2]. On Base44 this is a database table drained by a backend function/Automation. The outbox is the durability mechanism of the boundary frame; idempotency keys stored in each row make the drain safe to re-run.

included: persisting intent before the call as an append-only outbox row
a worker draining and marking rows done
decoupling user latency from external latency
excluded: the DLQ for exhausted rows (its own node)
the scheduled Automation that hosts the drain (its own node)

pros.claim: Writing intent first means no external effect is ever lost to a crash, and the user action returns before the slow call completes
pros.example: queueing an Anki write instantly and draining it later so the user is not blocked while Anki is offline

cons.claim: The outbox adds a store and a worker to operate and introduces eventual-consistency lag between intent and effect
cons.example: a reminder that is queued now but not actually created in Google Calendar until the drain runs seconds or minutes later

failure_modes: calling the external service before persisting intent so a crash loses the effect
draining without the stored idempotency key so a re-drain double-applies
acceptance_tests: intent is persisted append-only before the external call, a worker drains and marks rows done, and a re-drain after a crash is shown safe via the stored idempotency key
revisit_triggers: eventual-consistency lag becomes user-visible and unacceptable
the outbox table grows without pruning
Base44 storage/queue limits are hit

base.update_signal: unacceptable lag or a Base44 storage limit changes the outbox design

nodes.definition: Handle messages that keep failing after their max retry budget (poison messages) by moving them out of the main queue into a DEAD-LETTER state (a flagged outbox status or separate table) for human review or a repair job, so one broken effect neither blocks healthy traffic nor retries forever [FACT — DLQ pattern; METHOD for the exact thresholds]. Each dead-lettered row keeps its payload, key, error, and attempt count for diagnosis. This is the terminal branch of the retry policy: retries exhaust into the DLQ rather than looping, and DLQ depth becomes an observability signal that something is persistently wrong.

included: moving max-retry-exceeded messages to a dead-letter state
keeping payload/key/error/attempts for diagnosis
DLQ depth as a health signal
excluded: the circuit breaker that prevents the failures upstream (its own node)
the metric consumer wiring (its own node)

pros.claim: Dead-lettering keeps one poison effect from blocking the queue or retrying forever, and preserves it for repair
pros.example: a malformed reminder payload parked in the DLQ while all other reminders continue to send

cons.claim: A DLQ that no one watches silently accumulates lost effects, so it only works with a consumer and alert
cons.example: reminders quietly dead-lettering for a week because nobody checks the DLQ depth

failure_modes: retrying a poison message forever and blocking the queue
dead-lettering with no alert so failures go unnoticed
acceptance_tests: messages exceeding the retry cap move to a dead-letter state with payload/key/error retained, the main queue keeps flowing, and DLQ depth is exposed as a monitored signal
revisit_triggers: the DLQ accumulates without triage
a recurring poison class needs a dedicated handler
the max-attempt threshold before dead-lettering is retuned

base.update_signal: DLQ accumulation or a recurring poison class changes the dead-letter handling

nodes.definition: Guard a persistently failing or slow dependency with a circuit breaker: after a failure threshold, OPEN the breaker to fail fast (skip calls, return a degraded result) for a cooldown, then HALF-OPEN a trial call before closing — so a downed service does not exhaust timeouts, pile up retries, or cascade into the whole app [FACT — circuit-breaker pattern; this is the runtime form of sysloops' degraded mode per SPECIALIST_LIST §B2]. It composes with retries: retries handle blips, the breaker handles sustained outages. Optional/ban-risk integrations like WAHA WhatsApp default OFF and degrade silently [SIGNAL — WAHA account-ban risk per EXTERNAL_RECON §4/§Cross-cutting], so a WAHA outage must never block core study flows.

included: open/half-open/closed breaker states and cooldown
fail-fast degraded mode for a downed dependency
optional integrations (WAHA) defaulting off and degrading silently
excluded: the retry schedule for transient blips (its own node)
the DLQ for individual poison messages (its own node)

pros.claim: A breaker stops a downed dependency from exhausting timeouts and cascading, and lets the app degrade instead of stall
pros.example: Ollama Cloud being unreachable so the breaker opens and study continues without live LLM grading rather than hanging

cons.claim: A mis-tuned breaker either trips too eagerly (denying a recovering service) or too late (letting damage accumulate)
cons.example: a breaker with too low a threshold opening on a single slow call and disabling a healthy integration

failure_modes: no breaker so a downed service exhausts timeouts and blocks the app
a required flow depending on an optional ban-risk integration like WAHA
acceptance_tests: the breaker opens after a failure threshold and fails fast, half-opens a trial before closing, degrades gracefully, and optional/ban-risk integrations (WAHA) default off and never block core flows
revisit_triggers: the breaker trips too eagerly or too late
an integration's availability profile changes
a WhatsApp ban or WAHA outage exercises the degraded path

base.update_signal: a mis-timed trip or a changed availability profile changes the breaker tuning

nodes.definition: Bound every external call with an explicit per-call timeout, and keep the sum of a request's attempts (including backoff waits) UNDER the enclosing Base44 backend-function execution budget so a slow dependency cannot hang the function until the platform kills it mid-effect [FACT — deadline-budget discipline; the exact Base44 function execution limit is UNKNOWN in recon]. When the work legitimately needs longer than the budget (large Tripo 3D generation, a full nightly pipeline), move it off the synchronous path into the outbox/Automation rather than stretching the timeout. [UNKNOWN — Base44 per-function max execution time and rate limits; METHOD: measure in-app or check docs.base44.com backend-function limits before setting budgets.]

included: a per-call timeout on every external call
keeping total attempt time under the function execution budget
moving over-budget work to the async outbox/Automation
excluded: the backoff schedule inside the budget (its own node)
the outbox mechanics (its own node)

pros.claim: A per-call timeout under the function budget prevents a slow dependency from being killed mid-effect by the platform
pros.example: capping an Ollama call at a few seconds so a hung request fails cleanly instead of the whole function timing out

cons.claim: The real Base44 execution and rate limits are unknown here, so the budget is a placeholder until measured, and too-tight timeouts abort legitimately slow calls
cons.example: a Tripo generation aborted by a too-short timeout when it simply needed the async path

failure_modes: no per-call timeout so a slow call hangs until the platform kills the function mid-write
stretching a synchronous timeout instead of moving long work to the async path
acceptance_tests: every external call has a per-call timeout, the summed attempt time stays under the function budget, over-budget work is routed to the outbox/Automation, and the unknown Base44 limits are flagged with a METHOD to obtain them
revisit_triggers: Base44's real execution/rate limits become known
a function is killed mid-effect by the platform
a legitimately long job needs the async path

base.update_signal: learning Base44's real limits or a mid-effect kill changes the budget

nodes.definition: Base44 backend functions run custom TypeScript on Deno in an isolated environment for business logic, third-party API calls with protected credentials, webhooks, and custom endpoints [FACT-source: EXTERNAL_RECON §6]. They are the ONLY place a Base44 cloud app can hold secrets and reach external services, so every external call in this system (Ollama, Google, Tripo, WAHA, GitHub, and the localhost-bridge hop to Anki) originates in a backend function — never from the client, which cannot be trusted with keys and cannot reach private services. All reliability primitives (keys, backoff, outbox drain, breakers, timeouts) are implemented inside these functions.

included: Deno-isolate backend functions as the host for external calls
why external calls must not run client-side
backend functions as the container for the reliability primitives
excluded: the scheduling of functions as Automations (its own node)
the Secrets they read (its own node)

pros.claim: Centralizing every external call in backend functions is the only place secrets are safe and private services are reachable, and gives one place to apply the reliability primitives
pros.example: an Ollama call made from a backend function with the key injected server-side rather than exposed in client JavaScript

cons.claim: All external logic funnels through the Deno isolate, whose execution and concurrency limits (UNKNOWN here) bound what a single function can do
cons.example: a heavy fan-out of external calls in one function bumping into an unknown Deno-isolate limit

failure_modes: making an external call or holding a secret in client code
assuming unlimited execution inside a Deno-isolate function
acceptance_tests: every external call originates in a Deno backend function with server-side secrets, no external call or key lives in client code, and the reliability primitives are placed inside these functions
revisit_triggers: Base44 changes its backend-function runtime or limits
a call is found running client-side
a function hits an isolate execution limit

base.update_signal: a Base44 runtime change or a client-side call discovery revises the hosting rule

nodes.definition: Base44 Automations run backend functions on SCHEDULES or on database create/update/delete EVENTS [FACT-source: EXTERNAL_RECON §6]. This is the runtime that turns the app's runPipeline into a real recurring loop — the nightly analysis pipeline, the outbox drain, reminder dispatch, and model-list refresh all become scheduled Automations, and event-triggered Automations react to new records (e.g. a graded voice answer arriving). Because a schedule can fire while a prior run is still going or re-fire after a crash, every Automation body MUST be idempotent and guarded against overlapping execution, inheriting sysloops' idempotency rule.

included: schedule-triggered and DB-event-triggered Automations
hosting the nightly pipeline, outbox drain and reminder dispatch
the idempotent-and-overlap-guarded requirement
excluded: the specific nightly-pipeline analytics (owned by sysloops)
the outbox mechanics themselves (its own node)

pros.claim: Automations give the sysloops loop and the outbox drain a real scheduler without standing infrastructure
pros.example: a nightly Automation running the analysis pipeline and a frequent Automation draining the reminder outbox

cons.claim: Scheduled re-fires and overlaps mean a non-idempotent Automation body can double-apply or corrupt state, and Base44's scheduling guarantees are not fully documented here
cons.example: two overlapping nightly runs both re-sending the same reminders because the body was not overlap-guarded

failure_modes: a non-idempotent Automation double-applying on re-fire or overlap
assuming exactly-one scheduled invocation without a lock
acceptance_tests: schedule and DB-event triggers are described, the pipeline/drain/dispatch are hosted as Automations, and every Automation body is idempotent and overlap-guarded
revisit_triggers: Base44 changes its scheduling semantics or guarantees
overlapping runs are observed
a needed trigger type is unsupported

base.update_signal: a scheduling-semantics change or an observed overlap changes the Automation design

nodes.definition: User-provided API keys (Ollama, Tripo, WAHA, Google) are stored as Base44 per-app Secrets (environment variables) and read ONLY inside backend functions to call the external API; external services do not let Base44 access credentials automatically, so the user pastes the key and Base44 injects it at call time, never exposing it to the client [FACT-source: EXTERNAL_RECON §6]. For Ollama Cloud specifically the key is created at ollama.com/settings/keys and sent as an Authorization: Bearer header; keys do not expire but are revocable [FACT-source: EXTERNAL_RECON §1]. Secrets are the credential-handling foundation; their lifecycle (rotation, non-leakage) is a separate discipline.

included: storing pasted user keys as per-app Secrets read only server-side
the paste-and-inject model (services do not auto-share creds)
the Ollama Bearer-key specifics
excluded: the rotation/revocation/non-leakage lifecycle (its own node)
the OAuth flow for Google, which is not a pasted key (its own node)

pros.claim: Per-app Secrets keep user keys server-side and out of client code while still letting backend functions authenticate to each service
pros.example: injecting OLLAMA_API_KEY into a backend function as a Bearer header without the browser ever seeing it

cons.claim: Secrets are only as safe as the surrounding discipline: a key logged, printed in an error, or committed to the synced repo leaks it
cons.example: an unhandled error echoing the full Authorization header into logs a support view can read

failure_modes: exposing a Secret to the client or in an error/log
confusing a pasted-key service with an OAuth service that needs consent instead
acceptance_tests: user keys are stored as per-app Secrets read only inside backend functions, the paste-and-inject model is stated, the Ollama Bearer specifics are cited, and no Secret is ever exposed to the client

a service switches from key-based to OAuth auth
Base44 changes its Secrets model

base.update_signal: a leaked Secret or a shift to OAuth changes the credential handling

nodes.definition: Base44 AI agents are defined as JSONC config files under base44/agents/, synced via the Base44 CLI [FACT-source: EXTERNAL_RECON §6]. This is the declarative RUNTIME definition of the managing agent whose DUTIES and DOCTRINE sysloops owns — the JSONC files wire the agent's behavior into the app, and because they are files, they are reviewable and version-controllable through the GitHub sync. The managing agent's runtime therefore lives as: agent JSONC (definition) + backend functions (its external actions) + Automations (its schedule) + Secrets (its credentials), with sysloops supplying what it should do.

included: agents as JSONC under base44/agents/ synced via CLI
the agent JSONC + functions + Automations + Secrets runtime composition
the split from sysloops-owned duties/doctrine
excluded: the managing agent's duties and doctrine (owned by sysloops)
the GitHub sync mechanics (its own node)

pros.claim: Declaring agents as version-controllable JSONC makes the managing agent's runtime reviewable and reproducible rather than click-configured
pros.example: reviewing a diff to base44/agents/ in GitHub before it changes the agent's behavior

cons.claim: JSONC config plus CLI sync is only as safe as the review and sync discipline; a bad edit or an un-reviewed prompt-driven change ships behavior
cons.example: a Base44-side prompt edit auto-committing an agent change nobody reviewed before it ran

failure_modes: treating the agent JSONC as the agent's doctrine instead of just its runtime wiring
shipping an agent config change without review
acceptance_tests: agents are described as JSONC under base44/agents/ synced via the CLI, the runtime composition (JSONC + functions + Automations + Secrets) is stated, and duties/doctrine are deferred to sysloops
revisit_triggers: Base44 changes the agents config format or sync path
an un-reviewed agent change ships
sysloops revises the managing-agent duties the runtime must implement

base.update_signal: a Base44 agents-format change or an un-reviewed ship changes the runtime wiring

nodes.definition: Base44 offers 2-way GitHub sync: Base44 edits (including prompt-driven ones) auto-commit to the repo, and pushes to GitHub reflect back into Base44; it requires a Builder plan or higher [FACT-source: EXTERNAL_RECON §6]. This version-controls backend functions and agent JSONC, giving diffs, review, and rollback. Two hazards follow: bidirectional auto-commit can create edit conflicts or feedback churn between the two sides, and — critically — anything in the repo is NOT a safe place for secrets, so keys must stay in per-app Secrets and never be committed. The sync governs code and config, never credentials.

included: 2-way auto-commit/reflect-back sync (Builder plan+)
version control of functions and agent JSONC
the edit-conflict and never-commit-secrets hazards
excluded: the Secrets store the sync must exclude (its own node)
the agent JSONC content (its own node)

pros.claim: Two-way sync gives every backend function and agent config diffs, review and rollback via GitHub
pros.example: reverting a regression by rolling back a commit that then reflects back into Base44

cons.claim: Bidirectional auto-commit risks conflicts and churn, and the repo is the wrong home for secrets, so discipline is required to keep keys out
cons.example: a key accidentally hardcoded in a backend function getting auto-committed to GitHub

failure_modes: committing a secret into the synced repo
editing the same code on both sides and creating a sync conflict or loop
acceptance_tests: the 2-way sync and Builder-plan requirement are stated, functions/agent JSONC are version-controlled, and secrets are excluded from the repo with a never-commit rule
revisit_triggers: a secret is detected in the repo
sync conflicts or churn recur
Base44 changes the sync model or plan requirement

base.update_signal: a repo-secret detection or recurring sync churn changes the sync discipline

nodes.definition: Operate secrets over their whole lifecycle, not just at storage: rotate on a schedule or on suspected compromise, revoke promptly (Ollama keys are revocable in settings though they do not expire [FACT-source: EXTERNAL_RECON §1]), grant least privilege, and structurally prevent leakage — never log a secret, never echo it in an error, and never let it enter the GitHub-synced repo [FACT — standard secrets hygiene; the never-in-repo rule follows from BASE44_GITHUB_SYNC]. On a suspected leak the runbook is revoke-then-rotate-then-audit-the-repo. This lifecycle is what makes per-app Secrets actually safe rather than merely server-side.

included: rotation, revocation and least privilege
structural non-leakage (no logs, no errors, no repo)
the revoke-rotate-audit leak runbook
excluded: the initial storage of Secrets (its own node)
the GitHub sync mechanics (its own node)

pros.claim: A rotation and non-leakage lifecycle contains the blast radius of a compromised key and keeps secrets out of the synced repo
pros.example: revoking and reissuing an Ollama key within minutes of a suspected leak and confirming no commit contains it

cons.claim: Rotation without coordinated re-injection can briefly break calls, and non-leakage depends on disciplined logging everywhere
cons.example: rotating a key but forgetting to update the Secret so backend calls 401 until it is re-injected

failure_modes: logging or committing a secret
rotating a key without updating the Secret and breaking calls
acceptance_tests: the lifecycle covers rotation, revocation and least privilege, structurally forbids secrets in logs/errors/repo, and defines a revoke-rotate-audit runbook on a suspected leak
revisit_triggers: a secret is suspected leaked
a rotation breaks live calls
a vendor changes key expiry/revocation behavior

base.update_signal: a suspected leak or a rotation-induced outage changes the lifecycle

nodes.definition: Backend functions also serve as inbound endpoints/webhooks [FACT-source: EXTERNAL_RECON §6] — e.g. WAHA session-status/message events, or Google push notifications. Inbound events must be handled with the same rigor as outbound calls: VERIFY authenticity (signature/token where the sender provides one) before acting, and treat delivery as at-least-once so a duplicate webhook is de-duplicated by its event id and processed idempotently [FACT for the at-least-once property of webhooks; METHOD for per-vendor signature schemes, several UNKNOWN here]. WAHA specifically re-fires QR/session events, so a handler must be safe to receive the same event twice.

included: backend functions as verified inbound webhook endpoints
signature/token verification before acting
idempotent de-duplication of duplicate deliveries by event id
excluded: outbound call reliability (other reliability nodes)
the specific per-vendor signature schemes (integration KB / UNKNOWN)

pros.claim: Verifying and de-duplicating inbound events stops spoofed or replayed webhooks from driving duplicate or malicious effects
pros.example: processing a WAHA message event once by its id even though WAHA re-delivered it

cons.claim: Not every sender provides a signature and several vendor schemes are unknown here, so verification strength varies and must be researched per integration
cons.example: an inbound event whose only authenticity signal is a shared secret in the URL because no signature scheme is documented

failure_modes: acting on an unverified inbound webhook
processing a duplicate delivery as a new event
acceptance_tests: inbound events are received by backend functions, verified before action, and de-duplicated idempotently by event id, with unknown per-vendor signature schemes flagged for research
revisit_triggers: a spoofed or replayed webhook is observed
a vendor's signature scheme is documented or changed
a new inbound integration is added

base.update_signal: a spoof/replay incident or a documented vendor scheme changes webhook handling

nodes.definition: Run sysloops' nightly analysis pipeline and the outbox drain as idempotent Base44 Automations: each run reads the append-only logs, recomputes derived state, and drains queued external effects, written so a crash-then-rerun or an overlapping fire yields the same result — the runtime realization of sysloops' idempotent/append-only/degraded-mode loop across the network boundary [FACT — sysloops loop doctrine per SPECIALIST_LIST §A9/§B2; the Base44 Automation hosting is design synthesis, ESTIMATE]. Overlap is guarded with a run lock or a skip-if-running check, and a failed external step degrades rather than aborting the whole pipeline. This is where the reliability primitives and the platform meet.

included: hosting the nightly pipeline and outbox drain as idempotent Automations
overlap guarding with a lock/skip-if-running
degrading a failed external step instead of aborting
excluded: the pipeline's analytical steps (owned by sysloops)
the observability metrics it emits (its own node)

pros.example: a nightly run interrupted by a restart re-running cleanly to the same state instead of double-processing

cons.claim: Correct idempotency and overlap guarding is subtle, and a single missed non-idempotent step can corrupt derived state or double-fire effects
cons.example: a reminder-dispatch step that is not idempotent re-sending yesterday's reminders on a rerun

failure_modes: a non-idempotent pipeline step double-applying on rerun or overlap
aborting the whole pipeline when one external step fails instead of degrading
acceptance_tests: the pipeline and drain run as Automations that are idempotent over append-only logs, overlaps are guarded by a lock/skip, and a failed external step degrades rather than aborting the run

sysloops changes the pipeline step order
Base44 scheduling guarantees change

base.update_signal: a rerun/overlap corruption or a pipeline step-order change revises the runtime

nodes.definition: AnkiConnect binds 127.0.0.1:8765 and requires the desktop Anki app running, so a Base44 cloud backend CANNOT reach it directly — only via a bridge component on the user's own machine [FACT-source: EXTERNAL_RECON §2 and §Cross-cutting]. Reliability across this gap means: queue Anki writes in the outbox while Anki is offline (the common case), have the local bridge pull and apply them when Anki is WORKING, and make each apply idempotent via addNote with allowDuplicate/duplicateScope so a re-pull does not duplicate cards [FACT-source: EXTERNAL_RECON §2]. Workload influence (perDay limits, setDueDate, forgetCards) also flows through the bridge; desired-retention/FSRS params must be set in Anki's own UI [FACT-source: EXTERNAL_RECON §2].

included: the localhost-only constraint and the on-machine bridge
queue-while-offline and reconcile-when-WORKING with idempotent addNote
which workload levers flow through the bridge vs Anki's own UI
excluded: the full AnkiConnect action catalog (integration KB)
the FSRS scheduling science (owned by sched)

pros.claim: A queue-and-reconcile bridge makes Anki sync robust to the app being cloud and Anki being intermittently online
pros.example: cards authored today queued and applied idempotently the next time the user opens Anki on their laptop

cons.claim: The bridge is extra software on the user's machine and reconciliation is only as fresh as the user's Anki uptime, so sync is inherently eventual
cons.example: a week of queued writes not landing until the user next launches Anki

failure_modes: attempting a direct cloud-to-AnkiConnect call that can never reach localhost
re-applying queued writes without dedupe and duplicating cards
acceptance_tests: the localhost-only constraint and on-machine bridge are stated, writes queue while Anki is offline and reconcile idempotently via addNote allowDuplicate when WORKING, and the bridge-vs-Anki-UI split for workload levers is given
revisit_triggers: AnkiConnect changes its bind/security model
reconciliation drift or duplicate cards appear
the workload-lever set through AnkiConnect changes

base.update_signal: an AnkiConnect security change or reconciliation drift revises the bridge design

nodes.definition: Google Calendar/Tasks access to a user's private data requires per-user OAuth 2.0 consent, NOT an API key — so it uses Base44's OAuth connector flow, not a pasted Secret [FACT-source: EXTERNAL_RECON §3 and §Cross-cutting]. Runtime concerns: store and refresh the OAuth tokens, handle expiry/revocation by re-prompting consent rather than silently dropping effects, and choose the right surface for timed reminders — Calendar events with reminders.overrides (method popup/email, minutes 0-40320, max 5) give TIMED notifications, whereas the Tasks API discards the due time (date only), so timed reminders must use Calendar events [FACT-source: EXTERNAL_RECON §3]. There is no public Google Reminders API; reminders migrated into Tasks in 2023 [FACT-source: EXTERNAL_RECON §3].

included: per-user OAuth (not a key) via a connector flow
token storage/refresh and re-consent on revoke
Calendar events for timed reminders vs Tasks discarding the time
excluded: the full Calendar/Tasks field reference (integration KB)
the reminder-content/UX (owned by engage/uxguide)

pros.claim: Using OAuth and Calendar event reminders gives correct, consented, timed notifications where a pasted key or Tasks alone could not
pros.example: a study reminder as a Calendar event with a popup override 30 minutes before, under the user's OAuth grant

cons.claim: OAuth adds a consent/refresh lifecycle and revocation edge cases that a pasted key avoids, and the timed-reminder constraint forces Calendar over Tasks
cons.example: a revoked refresh token silently failing reminder creation until the user is re-prompted

failure_modes: trying to use an API key for private-calendar access that requires OAuth
using Tasks for a timed reminder and losing the time
acceptance_tests: private access is via per-user OAuth not a key, tokens are stored/refreshed with re-consent on revoke, and timed reminders use Calendar event overrides because Tasks discards the due time, with the no-public-Reminders-API fact stated
revisit_triggers: Google changes Calendar/Tasks auth or the reminders model

nodes.definition: Make in-app LLM calls resilient at runtime: pin model ids to non-retiring recommended alternatives, put a FALLBACK CHAIN behind the retry and circuit-breaker primitives (try model A, on persistent failure degrade to B or to the built-in InvokeLLM), and track cost/latency per call [FACT for the primitives; ESTIMATE for the exact chain]. Ground the retirement handling: several Ollama Cloud models retire 2026-07-15, so build against recommended alternatives (kimi-k2.6, minimax-m3, glm-5.2, qwen3.5, deepseek-v4-flash, gemma4:31b) and refresh the live model list from https://ollama.com/api/tags or /v1/models rather than hardcoding a catalog; only two cloud models are active at a time [FACT-source: EXTERNAL_RECON §1 and §Cross-cutting]. Rate limits and pricing tiers are UNKNOWN in recon [METHOD: check ollama.com/cloud and account settings].

a fallback chain behind retries and the breaker
cost/latency tracking and the two-active-model constraint
excluded: deep model evaluation/drift science (owned by the model-ops KB slice)
prompt engineering and rubric design

pros.example: a retired Ollama model automatically falling back to a pinned recommended alternative with no user-visible outage

cons.claim: Fallback across models risks inconsistent output quality, and the unknown rate limits/pricing make cost control partly guesswork until measured
cons.example: a fallback model grading voice answers on a slightly different scale than the primary, skewing comparisons

failure_modes: hardcoding a model that retires 2026-07-15 and breaking mid-run
no fallback so a single provider failure disables all LLM features
acceptance_tests: models are pinned to non-retiring recommended alternatives and the live list is refreshed from the tags/models endpoint, a fallback chain sits behind retries and the breaker, cost/latency is tracked, and the unknown limits are flagged with a METHOD
revisit_triggers: a pinned model nears retirement
provider failures exercise the fallback
Ollama's real rate limits/pricing become known

nodes.definition: Give every external call and queue an observability snapshot: success rate, latency, retry count, breaker state, DLQ depth, and token cost — each a stored daily trend (not a point) with a threshold and a NAMED automatic action or human-visible flag, and any metric with no consumer is deleted, extending sysloops' snapshot/threshold/named-consumer metric governance across the network boundary [FACT — sysloops metric governance per SPECIALIST_LIST §A9/§B2; the per-call application is design synthesis]. This is how a persistently failing dependency, a rising 429 rate, or a growing DLQ becomes visible and actionable instead of silent, closing the observable leg of the boundary frame.

included: per-call/per-queue snapshots (success/latency/retry/breaker/DLQ/cost)
threshold plus named consumer per metric, deleting consumerless metrics
extending sysloops metric governance across the boundary
excluded: the analytics dashboards/charts (owned by viz)
the internal pipeline self-metrics (owned by sysloops)

pros.example: a rising DLQ depth crossing its threshold and raising a flag the user or a repair job acts on

cons.claim: Metrics cost storage and attention, and an over-instrumented system with unread metrics is worse than a few consumed ones

acceptance_tests: each external call/queue emits snapshot trends with a threshold and a named action or flag, consumerless metrics are deleted, and the governance is shown to extend sysloops' rule across the boundary

nodes.definition: Compose the recommended runtime stack, the go/no-go this KB builds toward. Go: every cross-boundary effect carries an idempotency key, is retried with jittered exponential backoff (transient errors only), is persisted in a durable outbox drained by an idempotent Base44 Automation, exhausts into a DLQ, is guarded by a circuit breaker and a per-call timeout under the function budget, runs inside a Deno backend function reading per-app Secrets, with inbound webhooks verified and de-duplicated, Anki reached via a localhost bridge queue, Google via OAuth with Calendar-event timed reminders, LLM calls pinned-plus-fallback, and every call observable with a named-consumer metric [design synthesis over the cited primitives and EXTERNAL_RECON facts]. No-go: never call AnkiConnect directly from the cloud, never commit a secret to the GitHub-synced repo, keep WAHA off by default (ban-risk [SIGNAL]), and never build against Ollama models retiring 2026-07-15. A mechanism earns a place only if it makes an effect durable, idempotent, or observable.

included: the go stack (keys+backoff+outbox+DLQ+breaker+timeout on backend functions/Automations with Secrets, Anki bridge, Google OAuth, model fallback, observability)
the no-gos (no direct cloud-Anki, no secrets in repo, WAHA off, no retiring models)
the durable/idempotent/observable acceptance rule
excluded: the integration API details and model-ops science (sibling KBs)
sysloops' loop doctrine it implements

pros.claim: The merged verdict commits to a coherent runtime that makes every cross-boundary effect durable, idempotent and observable on Base44, and explicitly refuses the unsafe shortcuts
pros.example: shipping the outbox+Automation+bridge stack while declining direct cloud-to-Anki and secrets-in-repo

cons.claim: The full stack is more machinery than a single-user app strictly needs day one, and several platform limits it assumes are UNKNOWN until measured
cons.example: building an outbox and DLQ before traffic ever justifies them, against unknown Base44 execution limits

acceptance_tests: the verdict states the go stack and the no-gos (no direct cloud-Anki, no secrets in the synced repo, WAHA off by default, no models retiring 2026-07-15) and the durable/idempotent/observable acceptance rule for every mechanism
revisit_triggers: a no-go is violated in implementation

edges.why_related: the durable/idempotent/observable objective is motivated by the concrete failure taxonomy
the ambiguous-outcome failure is exactly what idempotency keys make safe to retry
the transient-vs-terminal failure taxonomy is what the retry policy classifies
retries are only safe on mutations because they carry a stable idempotency key
the outbox is the durability mechanism the boundary frame calls for
each outbox row stores an idempotency key so the drain is safe to re-run
the DLQ is where retries terminate after exhausting the max-attempt cap
dead-lettering is a terminal status of an outbox row that keeps failing
the breaker handles sustained outages that retries alone would only amplify
a dependency outage in the taxonomy is what trips the breaker into degraded mode
timeouts and slow responses in the taxonomy are what the per-call budget bounds
backend functions are the platform host where the cross-boundary reliability work runs
an Automation is a backend function bound to a schedule or DB event
per-app Secrets are readable only inside backend functions
agent JSONC wires behavior whose external actions run as backend functions
the 2-way sync version-controls the backend functions' code
the rotation/non-leakage lifecycle operates on the stored per-app Secrets
the never-commit-secrets rule follows from the repo being 2-way synced
inbound webhooks are served by backend-function endpoints
duplicate webhook deliveries are de-duplicated by an event-id idempotency key
the sysloops pipeline and outbox drain are hosted as scheduled Automations
the scheduled Automation is what drains the durable outbox
idempotent keys make a re-fired or overlapping scheduled run safe
Anki writes are queued in the outbox while Anki is offline
reconciliation re-applies queued writes idempotently via addNote allowDuplicate
the OAuth token exchange and Calendar calls run inside backend functions
OAuth tokens and client credentials are held in the Secrets store
LLM calls are retried on transient provider errors under the backoff policy
the fallback chain trips through the breaker when a model provider is down
the scheduled runtime emits the per-call and per-queue snapshots that are monitored
DLQ depth is one of the named-consumer health signals
the verdict adopts the idempotent scheduled runtime as the loop host
the verdict includes the localhost bridge queue as the Anki path
the verdict includes pinned-plus-fallback LLM model-ops
the verdict requires every adopted mechanism to be observable via named-consumer metrics
retries push to keep trying a failing call while the breaker pushes to stop trying, trading recovery speed against dependency protection
edges.resolution_rule: let retries handle transient blips within the attempt cap but let the breaker override and fail fast once failures are sustained, so a downed dependency is protected rather than hammered

edges.why_related: the 2-way sync wants everything in the repo for version control while secrets must never enter the repo
edges.resolution_rule: version-control code and agent JSONC but keep every secret in the per-app Secrets store with a gitignore/scan so no credential is ever committed

edges.why_related: durable async queuing favors deferring slow work while a tight synchronous timeout favors finishing within the function budget
edges.resolution_rule: keep fast effects on the synchronous path under the timeout budget and move any effect that cannot finish in-budget onto the async outbox rather than stretching the timeout

edges.why_related: the failure-rate and latency metrics feed back into whether and when the breaker should trip

conflict_axes.name: durability_vs_latency
conflict_axes.description: Persisting intent in a durable outbox and reconciling asynchronously protects against loss but adds eventual-consistency lag versus a synchronous call that returns the real result immediately.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: queue effects that must not be lost or that face an offline dependency (Anki) and keep only fast, must-be-fresh reads synchronous

conflict_axes.name: retry_aggressiveness_vs_dependency_protection
conflict_axes.description: Aggressive retries recover from transient failures fast but amplify load on a struggling dependency, while a breaker protects the dependency at the cost of recovery speed.
poles: fail fast to protect the dependency
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: retry transient blips within a capped, jittered schedule but let the circuit breaker override on sustained failure

conflict_axes.name: at_least_once_vs_at_most_once
conflict_axes.description: At-least-once delivery never loses an effect but can duplicate it, while at-most-once never duplicates but can silently lose effects; exactly-once is unachievable over the network.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: choose at-least-once and make it safe with idempotency keys and server-side dedupe

conflict_axes.name: secret_convenience_vs_exposure
conflict_axes.description: Pasting a key as a plain Secret and using it freely is convenient but risks leakage via logs, errors, or the 2-way-synced repo.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: keep secrets server-side only, forbid them in logs/errors/repo, and rotate on suspected compromise

conflict_axes.name: cloud_reach_vs_localhost_only
conflict_axes.description: The cloud app wants to write to Anki directly but AnkiConnect is localhost-only and needs the desktop app running, forcing an on-machine bridge and eventual sync.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: never call AnkiConnect from the cloud; queue writes and reconcile through a local bridge when Anki is WORKING

conflict_axes.name: oauth_complexity_vs_pasted_key
conflict_axes.description: Google private-data access needs a full per-user OAuth consent/refresh lifecycle rather than the simpler pasted-key model used for Ollama/Tripo/WAHA.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: use OAuth where the service requires it (Google) and pasted Secrets where a key suffices, never conflating the two

conflict_axes.name: model_freshness_vs_stability
conflict_axes.description: Adopting the newest LLM tracks capability but risks building on a model scheduled for retirement, while pinning an older stable model risks it being retired out from under you.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: pin to non-retiring recommended alternatives, refresh the live model list, and keep a fallback so a retirement is a non-event

conflict_axes.name: schedule_re_fire_vs_idempotency
conflict_axes.description: Scheduled Automations may re-fire after a crash or overlap a prior run, so a convenient non-idempotent body risks double-applying effects.
poles: make every run idempotent and overlap-guarded
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: treat every Automation as at-least-once, make the body idempotent, and guard overlap with a lock or skip-if-running

conflict_axes.name: feature_reach_vs_ban_risk
conflict_axes.description: WAHA WhatsApp messaging extends reminder reach but automates an unofficial WhatsApp client with account-ban risk, so more reach means more risk to a core channel.
poles: keep WAHA optional and off by default
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: keep WAHA off by default, degrade silently on failure, and never let a core flow depend on it

edge_cases.description: A duplicate delivery double-applies an Anki note, creating two identical cards
edge_cases.trigger: a timed-out addNote is retried without a dedupe key
edge_cases.mitigation: attach a stable key and use addNote allowDuplicate/duplicateScope so the re-send is deduplicated

edge_cases.description: A retry storm on a non-retriable 4xx burns quota and masks a real fault
edge_cases.trigger: a permanent 400/401/403 is classified as retriable
edge_cases.mitigation: retry only timeouts/5xx/429 honoring Retry-After and surface terminal 4xx immediately

edge_cases.description: An ambiguous timeout leaves it unknown whether the external write landed
edge_cases.trigger: a write call times out with no acknowledgment
edge_cases.mitigation: make the write idempotent so a safe retry either completes it or dedupes to the original

edge_cases.description: A secret is committed into the GitHub-synced repo
edge_cases.trigger: a key is hardcoded in a backend function and auto-committed by the 2-way sync
edge_cases.mitigation: keep keys in per-app Secrets with gitignore/secret-scan, and on a leak revoke-rotate-audit

edge_cases.description: An Ollama Cloud model is retired 2026-07-15 while the app still calls it
edge_cases.trigger: a model id is hardcoded against a retiring model
edge_cases.mitigation: pin to recommended non-retiring alternatives, refresh the live model list, and fall back automatically

edge_cases.description: Anki is offline when a write is needed and the effect would be lost
edge_cases.trigger: a cloud write targets AnkiConnect while the desktop app is closed
edge_cases.mitigation: queue the write in the outbox and reconcile idempotently when the bridge reports Anki WORKING

edge_cases.description: A Google OAuth refresh token is revoked and reminders silently stop
edge_cases.trigger: the user revokes access or the token expires without re-consent
edge_cases.mitigation: detect the auth failure, surface a re-consent prompt, and do not silently drop the reminder effect

edge_cases.description: A timed reminder loses its time because it was created as a Google Task
edge_cases.trigger: the Tasks API is used for a time-specific reminder
edge_cases.mitigation: create timed reminders as Calendar events with reminder overrides, since Tasks discards the due time

edge_cases.description: A scheduled Automation overlaps a prior still-running run and double-processes
edge_cases.trigger: a schedule fires while the previous invocation has not finished
edge_cases.mitigation: make the body idempotent and guard overlap with a run lock or skip-if-running check

edge_cases.description: A poison message retries forever and blocks the outbox queue
edge_cases.trigger: a malformed or permanently failing effect never succeeds or exits
edge_cases.mitigation: move it to the dead-letter state after the max-attempt cap and keep healthy traffic flowing

edge_cases.description: A WAHA WhatsApp session is banned or fails, threatening a core reminder channel
edge_cases.trigger: WhatsApp Web automation trips a ban or the session drops
edge_cases.mitigation: keep WAHA off by default, degrade silently, and route reminders through Calendar as the reliable channel

edge_cases.description: A backend function is killed by the platform mid-effect on a slow external call
edge_cases.trigger: a call runs longer than the function execution budget
edge_cases.mitigation: set a per-call timeout under the function budget and move long work onto the async outbox/Automation

workflow.action: Frame the boundary and enumerate the failure model
workflow.description: State the durable/idempotent/observable objective and the timeout/duplicate/ambiguous-outcome taxonomy with at-least-once semantics
workflow.gate: the three properties and the failure taxonomy are stated and exactly-once is ruled out in favor of at-least-once plus idempotency

workflow.action: Assign idempotency keys to every external mutation
workflow.description: Attach a stable per-action key and prefer native dedupe (AnkiConnect allowDuplicate) with an app-side ledger fallback
workflow.gate: each mutation carries a stable reused key and a replay is shown to dedupe to the original effect

workflow.action: Add backoff retries, circuit breaker, and timeout budgets
workflow.description: Retry only transient errors with jittered exponential backoff under a cap and a per-call timeout, with a breaker for sustained outages
workflow.gate: the policy retries only timeouts/5xx/429, caps attempts, bounds each call under the function budget, and trips a breaker on sustained failure

workflow.action: Build the durable outbox and dead-letter path
workflow.description: Persist intent append-only before the call, drain with a worker, and dead-letter messages that exhaust retries
workflow.gate: intent is persisted before the call, the drain is re-run-safe via the stored key, and exhausted messages move to the DLQ without blocking

workflow.action: Put every external call in a Base44 backend function
workflow.description: Move all external calls and secret reads server-side into Deno backend functions, never client-side
workflow.gate: no external call or secret lives in client code and the reliability primitives run inside backend functions

workflow.action: Store user keys as per-app Secrets with a rotation lifecycle
workflow.description: Store pasted keys as Secrets read only server-side, and define rotation, revocation and never-in-repo non-leakage
workflow.gate: keys are Secrets read only inside functions, excluded from logs/errors/repo, with a revoke-rotate-audit runbook

workflow.action: Schedule the sysloops loop and drain as idempotent Automations
workflow.description: Host the nightly pipeline and outbox drain as schedule/event Automations that are idempotent and overlap-guarded
workflow.gate: the pipeline and drain run as Automations, are idempotent over append-only logs, and are guarded against overlap

workflow.action: Wire Anki via a localhost bridge queue
workflow.description: Route Anki writes through an on-machine bridge, queueing while offline and reconciling idempotently when WORKING
workflow.gate: no direct cloud-to-Anki call, writes queue while offline, and reconciliation dedupes via addNote allowDuplicate

workflow.action: Wire Google via OAuth and LLM model-ops fallback
workflow.description: Use per-user OAuth with Calendar-event timed reminders, and pin-plus-fallback LLM models behind retries and the breaker
workflow.gate: Google uses OAuth with Calendar timed reminders, and LLM calls pin non-retiring models with a fallback chain

workflow.action: Add named-consumer metrics and issue the stack verdict
workflow.description: Emit per-call/per-queue metrics with thresholds and consumers, then commit to the go stack and the no-gos
workflow.gate: every call is observable with a named consumer and the verdict states the go stack and the no-gos (no direct cloud-Anki, no secrets in repo, WAHA off, no retiring models)

dominance_rules.rule: Idempotency dominates retry: never retry a mutation without a key
dominance_rules.rationale: a retry of a non-idempotent write duplicates the effect on the common ambiguous-timeout case
dominance_rules.trigger: a mutation is about to be retried
dominance_rules.action: attach a stable idempotency key or use native dedupe before allowing any retry

dominance_rules.rule: The circuit breaker dominates retries on a sustained outage
dominance_rules.rationale: continued retries against a downed dependency exhaust timeouts and cascade instead of recovering
dominance_rules.trigger: failures to a dependency exceed the breaker threshold
dominance_rules.action: open the breaker, fail fast, and degrade until a half-open trial succeeds

dominance_rules.rule: The durable outbox dominates fire-and-forget for any must-not-lose effect
dominance_rules.rationale: a crash between action and call loses an un-persisted effect
dominance_rules.trigger: an external effect that must not be lost is about to be sent
dominance_rules.action: persist intent append-only first and drain it with a worker

dominance_rules.rule: The Secrets store dominates hardcoding or committing keys
dominance_rules.rationale: a key in code or the 2-way-synced repo leaks it
dominance_rules.trigger: a credential is about to be placed in code or config
dominance_rules.action: store it as a per-app Secret read only inside backend functions and keep it out of the repo

dominance_rules.rule: The localhost bridge dominates any direct cloud-to-Anki attempt
dominance_rules.rationale: AnkiConnect is localhost-only and needs the desktop app, so a cloud call can never reach it
dominance_rules.trigger: a write to Anki is required from the cloud
dominance_rules.action: queue it and reconcile through an on-machine bridge when Anki is WORKING

dominance_rules.rule: OAuth dominates a pasted key for Google private-data access
dominance_rules.rationale: private calendars require per-user OAuth consent, not an API key
dominance_rules.action: run the OAuth consent/refresh flow rather than storing an API key

dominance_rules.rule: Calendar events dominate Tasks for timed reminders
dominance_rules.rationale: the Tasks API discards the due time so a Task cannot carry a timed notification
dominance_rules.action: create a Calendar event with reminder overrides instead of a Task

dominance_rules.rule: A pinned non-retiring model dominates a retiring one
dominance_rules.rationale: a hardcoded retiring model breaks when it is retired mid-run
dominance_rules.trigger: an LLM call selects a model
dominance_rules.action: pin to a recommended non-retiring alternative and keep a fallback

dominance_rules.rule: A metric with a named consumer dominates an unconsumed one
dominance_rules.rationale: an unread metric is cost without signal and hides the ones that matter
dominance_rules.action: give it a threshold and a named action or delete it, per sysloops metric governance

anti_rework_rules.rule: Choose the idempotency-key scheme before writing any external mutation
anti_rework_rules.prevents: retrofitting dedupe onto a history of double-applied writes

anti_rework_rules.rule: Classify retriable-vs-terminal errors before adding retries
anti_rework_rules.prevents: retry storms on permanent errors that burn quota and must be unwound

anti_rework_rules.rule: Put external calls behind backend functions from the start, never client-side
anti_rework_rules.prevents: ripping leaked keys and unreachable private-service calls out of client code later

anti_rework_rules.rule: Set up per-app Secrets and repo secret-scanning before enabling 2-way GitHub sync
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a committed credential that must be revoked, rotated, and scrubbed from history

anti_rework_rules.rule: Make scheduled Automations idempotent and overlap-guarded before scheduling them
anti_rework_rules.prevents: double-applied effects from re-fires and overlaps discovered in production

anti_rework_rules.rule: Build the Anki path as a queue-and-reconcile bridge from the outset
anti_rework_rules.prevents: reworking a direct-call design that can never reach localhost from the cloud

anti_rework_rules.rule: Pin LLM model ids to non-retiring alternatives before building calls
anti_rework_rules.prevents: an outage when a hardcoded model is retired on its scheduled date

anti_rework_rules.rule: Give every metric a threshold and a consumer when first emitted
anti_rework_rules.prevents: an instrumentation sprawl that is later pruned and re-scoped

iteration_protocol.trigger: an Ollama Cloud model nears its retirement date
iteration_protocol.action: swap to a pinned recommended alternative and re-test the fallback chain
tighten the idempotency key derivation and the server-side dedupe window
retune the backoff schedule and the circuit-breaker thresholds

iteration_protocol.trigger: a secret is suspected leaked or found in the repo
iteration_protocol.action: revoke, rotate, and audit the synced repository history

iteration_protocol.trigger: Base44's real function execution and rate limits become known
iteration_protocol.action: set timeout budgets and Automation cadences from the measured limits
triage the poison class and add a dedicated handler or fix

iteration_protocol.trigger: the Anki bridge reconciliation drifts or duplicates appear
iteration_protocol.action: add or tighten a state-reconciliation pass on the bridge

priority_rationale: The boundary frame and failure model come first because they decide the target (durable, idempotent, observable) and the delivery semantics (at-least-once made safe) every mechanism serves; idempotency keys, backoff retries, the durable outbox, dead-letter, circuit breaker and timeout budgets follow as the reliability primitives; the Base44 platform nodes (backend functions, Automations, Secrets, agents-JSONC, GitHub sync) and secrets-rotation and webhook handling supply the runtime host and its guardrails; the managing-agent runtime nodes (scheduled loop, Anki bridge, OAuth/model-ops) compose primitives and platform into the concrete integrations; and observability plus the stack verdict come last because they close the observable leg and commit the go/no-go over everything upstream.
